clue.text: Worn by horses, rubbed by antiquarians

definitions.meaning: decorative metal plaques hung on a carthorse's harness
engraved memorial plates in church floors, copied by rubbing paper with wax

explanation.definitionFit: Horse brasses are harness ornaments, and monumental brasses in churches are what enthusiasts copy by brass-rubbing.

clue.text: Their products are moved in the backyard

definitions.text: Their products are moved in the backyard

parts.words: Their products are moved in the backyard
parts.note: read as makers of ale and beer, whose casks are rolled and loaded onto drays in the yard behind the works

explanation.definitionFit: Makers of beer see their barrels shifted about the yard at the back of the brewery before delivery.

parts.note: points to the George Bernard Shaw play 'The ... Cart', a political comedy of 1928

explanation.surface: Something hauled away in a wagon by a man named Shaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's play is titled The Apple Cart, so the fruit is the thing that goes in his cart.

parts.note: in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, the man warning of the Ides of March is dismissed with 'He is a dreamer; let us leave him'

explanation.surface: Julius Caesar dismisses someone as a mere daydreamer.
explanation.definitionFit: A seer foretelling the future warns Caesar of the Ides of March and is brushed off as a fantasist.

parts.note: read as a town that is a credit to the old county of Middlesex, west of London

explanation.surface: Something valuable found in the English county of Middlesex.
explanation.walkthrough: Middlesex was the historic county covering much of west London; this Thames-side town lay in it.
explanation.definitionFit: The town on the Thames was a notable place within the county, a holding of Middlesex.

clue.text: Game fellow, in spite of internal pain

definitions.text: Game fellow, in spite of internal pain

parts.words: Game fellow, in spite of internal pain
parts.note: read as a man after game birds and rabbits, who carries an ache within him

explanation.surface: A plucky chap who carries on despite a stomach ache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like 'plucky', but it means quarry; and the answer has ACHE inside it, the 'internal pain'.
explanation.definitionFit: An illegal hunter takes game from another's land, so he is literally a game fellow.

parts.note: the Metropolitan Police was founded in 1829 by Sir Robert Peel, and its officers were nicknamed after him

explanation.surface: A law or regulation that took effect in 1829.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Came into force' sounds like a statute taking effect; it means joining the police force.
explanation.definitionFit: Early London constables were nicknamed after Robert Peel, who set up the Metropolitan Police in 1829.

indicators.note: the word tenants loses the number it contains, ten, so it is left without a number

explanation.surface: Lodgers in a building without house numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unnumbered' removes TEN from TENANTS; read whole, the clue also describes the insects, countless occupants of a nest.
explanation.definitionFit: The insects are occupants of an anthill too many to count.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'Cosh a lout (anag.)' is an anagram instruction only, with no definition word anywhere in it, so no def can be given honestly.

definitions.meaning: noun sense: loud bangs, as of guns going off

explanation.definitionFit: Reports are both the bangs of firearms and pieces of news; 'Loud' stands for the noisy sense.

clue.text: Its devotees are a sly-looking lot

definitions.text: Its devotees are a sly-looking lot

parts.words: Its devotees are a sly-looking lot
parts.note: the people devoted to it are spies, who look furtive

explanation.surface: Followers of some cult appear shifty as a group.
explanation.walkthrough: The devotees are spies; the clue also suggests 'spy-looking', pointing at their trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Spying is the trade of secret agents, a famously furtive crowd.

parts.note: points to Alexandre Dumas's novel The Black ..., about breeding a dark bloom in Holland

explanation.surface: A dark bloom that appears in a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumas wrote The Black Tulip, about a quest to grow a black bulb flower.

parts.note: taken literally: equally good with both hands, so fair to both sides

explanation.definitionFit: Being impartial is a figurative sense of having both hands equal, which is what ambidexterity is.

parts.note: a blemish, and also the word that, followed by 'borough', names the Yorkshire seaside town of ...

explanation.surface: The emblem or sign of a town in Yorkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Scarborough is a seaside town in Yorkshire, northern England; its first part is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A scar is a mark left on the skin by a healed wound.

clue.text: Frank is able to take orders

definitions.text: Frank is able to take orders

parts.note: a common short form of the name Francis
able means can

explanation.surface: A man called Frank is fit to receive instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take orders' means joining a religious order; the order founded by St Francis of Assisi.
explanation.definitionFit: Friars of the order of St Francis take holy orders, and the name itself is Francis plus can.

parts.note: split as 'sees saws': one may see cutting tools at a hardware shop

explanation.surface: Something a customer might do in a hardware shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as 'sees saws' and the clue completes itself; an ironmonger is a British hardware shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it means one looks at cutting tools, which a shopper may do in a hardware store.

parts.note: 'big noise' means an important person, but also a bang; the temper of a volatile person is described as bursting out

explanation.surface: What kind of character an important person tends to have.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'big noise' is slang for a VIP; read literally it is a bang, which suggests a volatile temper.
explanation.definitionFit: A volatile, quick-tempered nature is said to be liable to burst out, like a bomb's noise.

clue.text: Shoots that might give, us sport

indicators.note: these letters could be rearranged to give something else, so they are to be shuffled

explanation.surface: Someone out hunting hopes the targets will provide entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoots' sounds like hunting, but it is the definition (new plant growth); 'might give' rearranges US SPORT.
explanation.definitionFit: New growths sprouting from a plant or seed are its young shoots.

clue.text: A step in a wise direction

indicators.note: the letters are given a new arrangement or direction, so they are to be reordered

explanation.surface: Taking a step towards doing the sensible thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'direction' rearranges A STEP IN; 'a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapient is a literary word for having great wisdom and discernment.

parts.note: points to Edgar Wallace's novel '... of the River', about a colonial officer in Africa

explanation.surface: An unusual person who lives by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like 'unusual', but it means a book: Edgar Wallace's Sanders of the River.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Sanders of the River is a district commissioner along an African river.

clue.text: Not a popular brand of jam

definitions.text: Not a popular brand of jam

parts.words: Not a popular brand of jam
parts.note: jam read as a road congestion, not a fruit preserve sold under a brand name

explanation.surface: A fruit preserve that does not sell well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jam' looks like the preserve; it is a hold-up of vehicles, which nobody likes.
explanation.definitionFit: A traffic jam is a kind of jam that no motorist welcomes.

parts.note: an extremist, pictured as having a cooling device, a fan, as his head, his attic

explanation.surface: An excitable person who is somehow calmer than expected.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer splits as FAN (a cooler) plus ATIC, close to 'attic', slang for the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A zealot is a hothead, an excitable extremist.

clue.text: He is in the front rank of players

definitions.text: He is in the front rank of players

parts.words: He is in the front rank of players
parts.note: read as a sports position: a player in the front line of a football or rugby team

explanation.surface: A top performer among actors or musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'front rank of players' suggests the leading actors; it means the front line of a team.
explanation.definitionFit: In football and rugby the attacking or scrummaging players at the front are the team's front line.

clue.text: Good if applied to one's own brains, bad to those of others

definitions.text: Good if applied to one's own brains, bad to those of others

parts.words: Good if applied to one's own brains, bad to those of others
parts.note: to rack one's brains is good, but beating someone else's head with clubs is assault

explanation.surface: Advice about thinking hard yourself versus interfering with others' minds.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'cudgel one's brains' means think hard; the weapons used on another's head are violence.
explanation.definitionFit: Short clubs are what you hit someone with, and the idiom uses them for thinking hard.

clue.text: No one is curtailed this time

indicators.note: curtailed means cut short at the tail, so the last letter of one goes

explanation.surface: Nobody has their tail docked at present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curtailed' removes the last letter of ONE, leaving ON; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Midday is a time of day, the hour of twelve o'clock.

clue.text: Does it describe one who thinks in a roundabout way?

definitions.text: Does it describe one who thinks in a roundabout way?

parts.words: Does it describe one who thinks in a roundabout way?
parts.note: a roundabout is a merry-go-round at a funfair, so a mind full of fairground rides

explanation.surface: Asking whether a word fits someone who reasons indirectly.
explanation.walkthrough: A roundabout is a British merry-go-round, a fairground ride; 'fair' means a funfair, though the answer means just.
explanation.definitionFit: An impartial person is just in judgement, which is the everyday sense of the word.

definitions.note: an adjective standing for the noun: forceful energy, vigour

indicators.note: a rendering is a performance or version, so the composer's name is played in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A powerful performance of a Verdi opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rendering of' rearranges VERDI; the definition stands for forceful energy.
explanation.definitionFit: Drive is vigour and determination, a forceful energy.

definitions.meaning: icy pellets falling from the sky, a cold kind of shower

explanation.definitionFit: Frozen pellets of rain fall in a cold storm, and to greet someone loudly is to call out a welcome.

indicators.note: in signals the name is found inside the word clerical, dressed in it like garb

explanation.surface: A young woman wearing a cleric's clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: The name sits inside 'clerical', wearing it like 'garb'.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is a woman's given name.

indicators.note: is in tells us the word his goes inside the word France

explanation.surface: A man's home is in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'place' looks like a home, but in old usage it names a district holding special legal privileges, such as a sanctuary; 'is in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically a franchise was a privileged territory or sanctuary with its own legal rights.

clue.text: A bill for munitions is a _ superficial matter

parts.note: a shell is an artillery projectile, a piece of munitions
AC is the abbreviation of account, a bill

explanation.surface: A government's spending on armaments is only a trivial matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'superficial matter' means surface stuff: the resin used to coat and varnish a surface; 'for' and 'is' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Lac resin is used as a varnish, a coating applied to the surface of wood.

parts.note: people who trip the light fantastic, moving lightly on their feet, rather than day-trippers

explanation.surface: Holiday day-trippers of some kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trippers' suggests holidaymakers; it means those who trip lightly on their toes.
explanation.definitionFit: People who dance move with light quick steps, which is to trip.
